title: “If I were the leader...”: Cultural framing in a group discussion about ethics.
venue: Centre for Research on Learning and Innovation

annotation.summary: Complex global problems need diverse teams of skilled knowledge and other workers to create solutions across discipline domains, cultural continuums and physical landscapes. Their active and productive participation in group knowledge creation needs skilful attention to the way they and others frame problems and conduct interactions. As educators, the way we design learning activities can influence the effectiveness of that participation, through raising learners’ awareness of the underlying values and beliefs that inform the way they connect with each other and co-construct knowledge objects. There will often be no simple or isolated solution to the issue at hand, as we recognise the interconnectedness of systems and ecologies. While traditionally leadership and decision-making have been situated within political or administrative circles, there is increasing focus on stakeholder engagement in managing change, often in consultation with professionals across multiple disciplines and locations. Inclusion of multiple perspectives is essential, but can be difficult to implement without an understanding of the way we make sense of others’ interactions, as communication contains meta-messages about their intention and position in relation to that which is being communicated. These meta-frames are built on deep sociocultural frameworks intimately connection with language and presentation of self in the face of others. Without deliberate attention to the different communicative strategies used by others, communication can break down and teamwork become less effective. The aim of this study is to observe a group interaction and identify whether there are specific cultural framing/s that the participants consciously or unconsciously enact during the activity. If there are particular ways of knowing and doing that can be demonstrated through analysis, this may help us to create learning activities that foster more effective teamwork. Emerging work around communicative flexibility and epistemic fluency can inform practices that integrate personal and professional behaviours across boundaries to active existing resources, spending lesson time more usefully and providing learners with interactional skills that will continue to assist them in their trajectories of lifelong learning.
